sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We believe active recall and guided discovery are far more effective than passive reading. We were inspired by the Socratic method to build an AI tutor that doesn't just give answers but asks the right questions.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Agora is a voice-first, multimodal AI tutor that you study with. You upload your notes, PDFs, or even photos of your lecture scribbles, and then talk to the tutor via a push-to-talk interface. It guides you through complex topics with Socratic questions, live analogies, and visual explanations on an infinite blackboard, all while tracking your "confused" topics to generate quizzes later.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Agora's backend is a stateful LangGraph agent (run on FastAPI with Python) that orchestrates Gemini 2.5 Pro for reasoning and multimodal vision. We use Qdrant as a vector database for RAG on uploaded documents and to store the student's long-term "memory". The frontend is a Next.js app using Tldraw for the interactive blackboard, all connected in real-time via Socket.IO for streaming voice and visual commands.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Integrating the stateful LangGraph agent with a real-time WebSocket connection was our biggest challenge, leading to message loops until we correctly managed listeners in our React hook. We also had to debug tricky API mismatches in Tldraw (like .clear() vs. .deleteShapes()) and fine-tune our RAG node's logic to prevent it from retrieving old documents in response to simple greetings like "hi".

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are incredibly proud of achieving a full, end-to-end multimodal loop. The system successfully takes a user's voice, transcribes it, routes it through the AI agent, retrieves context from a vector DB, and responds with both synthesized speech and visual actions on the Tldraw canvas. Seeing the AI draw a note on the blackboard that it "thought" of, based on our prompt, was the magic moment.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned that a powerful model like Gemini 2.5 Pro is only as good as the robust system you build around it; our Socratic system prompt had to be heavily revised with guardrails to handle "idk" and bad RAG retrievals. We also learned that state management is the most critical piece of a complex agent, which made LangGraph the perfect tool. Finally, we say that RAG (like ingesting handwritten notes from a photo) is not just a demo - it's practical and powerful.

sections.heading: What's next for Agora Socrates
sections.text: The next step is to make the tutor proactive. We plan to implement a spaced repetition feature that uses the AI's memory of "confused topics" to generate review quizzes at the start of a new session. We also want to implement "self-explanation scoring," where the AI asks the user to explain a concept in their own words and then scores their explanation against the original document context. sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Innovation shouldn't come with a surprise bill. As developers rushing to build the next big thing, we often treat AI as a magic wand. But unlike memory or CPU cycles, AI API calls cost real money—and those costs are currently invisible until the invoice arrives. We realized that to truly innovate sustainably, engineers need financial intuition built directly into their tools. Whether you're a bootstrapper protecting your runway or an enterprise scaling a unicorn, you can't afford to be blind to your burn rate. Quota was born to make cost a first-class citizen in the development lifecycle, bridging the gap between "move fast" and "don't go broke."

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Quota is a real-time financial intelligence suite for modern engineering. It catches "financial bugs" before they ship. VS Code Extension (The Linter for your Budget) : Acts as a real-time cost copilot. It scans your code as you type, flagging expensive API calls (like legacy GPT-4 usage) with a live "heatmap" and suggesting cheaper, faster alternatives instantly. It even features a "Bankruptcy Countdown" that predicts your runway based on your projected scale. Web Sandbox (The Architectural Playground) : A drag-and-drop canvas for system design. Sketch out your architecture, and Quota's AI agent predicts the infrastructure and AI costs before you write a single line of code. It helps you design for scale from Day 1.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We engineered a dual-pronged system to cover the entire development lifecycle: The Extension : Built with TypeScript and the VS Code API . We implemented a custom AST parser to identify complex API usage patterns and a heuristic algorithm to estimate token usage in real-time. We engineered a "One-Click Fix" system that programmatically refactors code to use optimized models. The Dashboard : A Next.js + React Flow canvas powered by a FastAPI backend. We integrated Google Gemini via LangChain and FAISS vector stores to create a RAG-powered "AI Architect" that understands both system design and pricing models.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The Speed vs. Depth Trade-off : Real-time cost estimation is incredibly tricky. We had to balance the parser's speed (ensuring zero lag in the editor) with the depth of analysis required to find obfuscated API calls. Context Management : creating accurate architectural suggestions required fine-tuning our RAG system to give precise advice without hallucinating non-existent cloud services or pricing tiers.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Thinking outside the box by treating "Cost" as a code quality metric akin to linting errors. Building a fully functional AST-based refactoring engine that safely modifying user code. Integrating Gemini to provide intelligent architectural reasoning, not just generic autocomplete. Shipping a cohesive, polished tool that we actually use to optimize itself.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned that "hidden tech debt" is often financial. By visualizing the cost of our own project using Quota, we realized how quickly small architectural decisions—like choosing a slightly larger embedding model—compound into massive monthly bills at scale.

sections.heading: What's next for Quota
sections.text: We plan to expand Quota to track Cloud Infrastructure (AWS/GCP resources) and Database Compute costs. Our vision is to implement CI/CD checks that block pull requests if they exceed budget thresholds, effectively creating a firewall against accidental spending spikes.

sections.text: SignHero 🤟

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Over 48 million Americans are deaf or hard of hearing, yet ASL literacy remains low among the hearing population. We wanted to make learning ASL fingerspelling fun, accessible, and engaging —the same way Guitar Hero made learning rhythm patterns addictive. The breakthrough idea: What if we could gamify sign language learning with real-time AI detection and rhythm-based gameplay?

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: SignHero is a rhythm game that teaches ASL fingerspelling through webcam-powered gameplay: Mode Description 🎸 Song Game Sign along to beatmaps synced with music—notes scroll down a Guitar Hero-style highway 📚 Training Mode Step-by-step practice with visual hand pose hints ⏱️ Testing Mode Timed challenges to measure proficiency 🕹️ Whack-A-Sign Arcade-style reflex game for quick recognition The AI watches your webcam, detects which ASL letter you're signing in real-time (~30-50ms latency), and scores your accuracy with combo multipliers, streak celebrations, and visual effects.

sections.heading: How We Built It
sections.text: 🧠 Machine Learning Pipeline! For this we build a custom model based on the mobileneyb2 cnn as our backbone. The model has 2 main parts, the feature extraction and the classification! For extraction we have 32 channels, and use 5 specialized attention layers! We also have a custom classifier with a standard RELU activation function and filter that finalizes converting the single frame into 26 different classes! We used various modified training data in order to be able to have a consistent model with different angles to make this compatible with various people to remove bais and more! There is alot more documentation on architecture training preprocessing and more in the folder here: https://github.com/MsMarion/ASL-Fun-Training/tree/main/Base%20test/Sign-Language-Recognition/documentation Webcam Frame → MediaPipe (hand landmarks) → Feature Extraction → MobileNetV2 CNN → Letter Prediction MediaPipe Hands detects 21 hand landmarks from webcam frames Landmarks are drawn as a feature mask on a black background MobileNetV2 (trained on ASL alphabet data) classifies the pose into A-Z Both original and mirrored images processed; max confidence used 🎮 Full-Stack Architecture Layer Technology Frontend Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4 Animation Framer Motion (smooth transitions, particle effects) API tRPC + React Query for type-safe data fetching Database MongoDB via Prisma ORM ML Server FastAPI (Python) serving PyTorch model Hand Tracking MediaPipe for real-time landmark

sections.heading: Challenges We Faced
sections.text: ⚡ Latency Optimization Real-time gameplay requires sub-100ms detection. We achieved ~30-50ms by: Using binary WebSocket protocol for frame transmission Running MediaPipe + MobileNetV2 on separate threads Processing both original and mirrored hand poses for better accuracy 🎯 Sign Recognition Accuracy Hand signs are subtle—slight angle changes affect predictions. We improved accuracy by: Training on hand landmark feature masks rather than raw images Using mirrored predictions (max of both) to handle left/right hands Implementing confidence thresholds to filter noise 🎵 Timing Synchronization Syncing game timing with AI predictions was tricky: Note timing window: [noteTime - 2.0s, noteTime + 0.8s] Perfect window: [noteTime - 0.3s, noteTime + 0.3s] We buffer predictions and match them against note windows in real-time.

sections.heading: What We Learned
sections.text: MediaPipe is incredibly fast for hand tracking (~5-10ms) MobileNetV2 provides a great balance of accuracy vs. speed for real-time inference Building rhythm games requires careful attention to input latency Framer Motion makes complex animations surprisingly approachable

devpost_page.title: Atlas
devpost_page.tagline: 3D learning environments for the modern era.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Education has always struggled to make history and science feel real. Reading about life in an Ancient Chinese Village or how photosynthesis works in a textbook is passive. You're told what happened/happens, not shown it. We were inspired by the idea that immersive 3D environments could transform learning from memorization into genuine exploration, and that an AI guide embedded inside those worlds could answer questions the way a knowledgeable human standing next to you would.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Atlas lets you type any historical event or scientific concept and instantly step inside a generated 3D world built around it. Once inside, an AI Guide speaks and responds to your questions in real time, grounding every answer in the specific scene you're exploring. You can click on individual objects to focus on them, ask follow-up questions, and for STEM scenes, interact with guided experiments like a photosynthesis cycle that responds to your actions.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Atlas is built on a Next.js frontend with a Node/Express backend. On the client, we render worlds with Spark + Three.js for real-time navigation, interaction, and HUD overlays. We use World Labs’ Marble model to generate immersive 3D Gaussian Splat worlds from text prompts, Google Gemini to power the scene interpretation and conversational Historical Guide, and ElevenLabs to synthesize the guide’s spoken responses. The scene graph system structures each world into labeled, queryable elements that give the AI precise spatial and historical context for every answer.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Getting the AI guide to stay grounded in the scene, rather than hallucinating people or objects that weren't there, required careful prompt engineering around the scene graph. Streaming 3D Gaussian Splat assets reliably while keeping the chat experience responsive was technically tricky, as world generation can take several minutes. In addition, the world generation can remain very blurry even with user's images, which can make the world building limiting. Integrating ElevenLabs TTS in a single chat round-trip without blocking the text response also required separating the audio pipeline carefully.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We're proud that the full loop works end-to-end: you type a prompt, a real 3D world generates around it, and a voice-enabled AI guide answers your questions from inside that world with historically accurate detail. The STEM experiment mode felt very innovative to teach science through interaction rather than instruction.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Building Atlas, we looked deep into Gaussian Splatting, which that enabled us to create photorealistic worlds. Integrating Spark, World Labs' viewer for Gaussian Splat scenes, taught us how to embed and control splat rendering inside a web environment, and how the underlying .spz asset format packages splat data for streaming delivery. On the 3D web side, working with Three.js sharpened our understanding of scene graphs, camera controls, and how to layer interactive UI elements on top of a live 3D canvas without fighting the renderer.

sections.heading: What's next for Atlas
sections.text: We want to improve the graphics of the 3D world generation. Even with Gaussian Splat creating a realistic world to explore with one image, it can be more meaningful to create a larger world. In addition, we want to integrate VR compatibility so that users can have a more immersive experience and utilize body motion to interact with the world easily.

devpost_page.title: SonoRocky
devpost_page.tagline: Narrating the world for the visually-impaired.

sections.heading: I. Inspiration
sections.text: Our inspiration came from a teammate who witnessed his dormmate, who was visually impaired, struggling to navigate campus using only a mobility cane. Although his cane helps detect nearby obstacles, it provides limited information about the surrounding environment, making independent navigation challenging. [Research] shows that 7% of visually impaired and/or blind respondents experienced non-superficial injuries every month due to hazards and trips. Furthermore, 13% of respondents reported having head-level injuries that resulted in stitches and dental care every month. These experiences inspired us to develop technology that helps our community members with visual impairments to detect obstacles, avoid collisions, and navigate campus more safely and independently.

sections.heading: II. What It Does?
sections.text: SonoRocky includes two major elements: 1) Our Vision-to-Language application, and 2) a Mobility Cane System to detect distances. The Vision System gathers data from a phone camera and the Mobility Cane System to generate a visual-to-audio output that uses natural spoken language to warn vision-impaired persons about their surroundings, as UW research has indicated they possess superior hearing and perception. It also allows individuals to prompt the application with questions about what's in front of them and to read text on walls, to which the model can respond with detailed descriptions. The Mobility Cane System uses an acoustic sensor to detect obstacles in surrounding areas. This data is sent to the Vision System, which converts distance measurements into a series of variable-frequency beeps heard by the individual using the app, warning them to slow down in their stride as they approach obstacles.

sections.heading: III. How We Built It?
sections.text: Perceptron's mk1.5 model was used for recognizing still-frame captures taken from the device camera at a dynamic FPS rate, which then returns a natural language description with customizable details and hazard alerts (< 2-second latency) ElevenLabs' TTS model was used for streaming real-time audio readouts of Perceptron's descriptions The backend server handles interacting with both APIs and can route communication with multiple devices each running its own frontend instance. It also receives POST packets from the ESP8266 with distance data and WiFi status info ESP8266 used for processing ultrasonic distance sensor data, which is transmitted over WiFi to the backend server Fusion 360 + Prusa MK4 to 3D print a housing for the prototype, which can clamp onto rods of varying diameters

sections.heading: IV. Challenges We Ran Into
sections.text: Limited access to hardware and tools for building our demo We needed a tilted angle for the ultrasonic sensor on the Mobility Cane System so that it faces perpendicular to the ground Balancing high-speed camera refresh rate while staying within API ratelimits Tuning the speed of generating the natural language outputs from our video feed, along with the level of detail in the descriptions CAD design for a good angle facing forward on the mobility cane

sections.heading: V. Accomplishments that We're Proud of
sections.text: We limit the character for the audio output for every scan for faster processing speed Prioritize possible hazards before introducing minor details of the surroundings Estimate the minimal amount of stairs to prevent accidental trips Hardware costs less than $15 to assemble

sections.heading: VI. What We Learned?
sections.text: Hardware/Software integration Things do not always go as we expected Optimization of features Software advice from our community mentors (huge shoutout to David from Perceptron!)

sections.heading: VII. What's Next for SonoRocky
sections.text: In order to bring our project to the next level, we decide to achieve our goal by improving the two systems. We want to build sunglasses for the Vision System, with two separate cameras, one looking forward and one looking down, a CPU and two speakers for audio output at the hooks of the sunglasses. The cameras were used to scan the surroundings and identify possible obstacles at a refresh rate of 120 FPS to give a safer condition for vision-impaired people. The forward-facing camera uses a wide-angle lens to capture as much information as possible, while the downward-facing camera estimates the steps between the incoming obstacles (e.g., stairs or uneven ground) with motion sensors to warn the person as he walks. Moreover, we want to complete the mobility cane system by making it fit different types of mobility canes with different lengths and diameters. Furthermore, the cane should not have only one sensor; we will implement several ToF sensors to detect the surroundings in multiple directions and angles, like a LiDAR. Lastly, we would also like to implement more features associated with maps and navigation into our project. We wanted our Vision System to be able to communicate with the user, through natural spoken languages, and be able to understand and execute commands. Nevertheless, location synchronisations will also help a lot in creating a map-level navigation system, so we can better locate and predict the possible surroundings of the user.

sections.heading: VIII. Why the Name?
sections.text: The prefix "Sono-" refers to the usage of sonar in navigation; while "Rocky" is a character in the film "Project Hail Mary" who has no eyes and navigates based on sounds, which resonates with the main aim of our project. Rocky also speaks in short, succinct phrases, just like our project 🪨.

devpost_page.title: WeCare
devpost_page.tagline: WeCare makes sure seniors take the right pill at the right time, and lets the people who care about them know they did.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Many seniors take a lot of medications every day. In Canada, 1 in 4 seniors were prescribed 10 or more different types of medications in 2021, and that rises to 36.4% for those 85 and older. Taking multiple drugs is linked to a higher risk of emergency visits and hospitalization. With that many pills, mistakes happen. When poison centres looked at medication errors in older adults, the most common were taking a medication twice, taking the wrong medication, and taking the wrong dose. These aren't small slip-ups: medication nonadherence accounts for more than 10% of older adult hospital admissions and nearly 25% of nursing home admissions, and in older adults the consequences can be more serious and harder to notice. Behind every senior is often a family member asking the same question every day: "Did Mom take her pills?" We wanted to build something that helps seniors take the right pill at the right time, without screens or complicated apps, and gives the people who care about them peace of mind. For the seniors, existing medication reminder apps simply do not work. Seniors often struggle with digital literacy, and apps are often overwhelming. That's why we built WeCare, on the senior's there is almost no interface, keeping it as easy to use as possible. We also 3D-printed a fun form factor to make the experience more fun!

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: WeCare makes sure seniors take the right pill at the right time and lets their family know they did. It reminds. At each scheduled time, WeCare speaks a friendly reminder with the senior's name and the caregiver's instructions, like "Good morning, Em! Time for your Lisinopril. Take it with a glass of water." It confirms. After taking their medication, the senior simply taps the touch sensor. WeCare plays a cheerful jingle and logs the dose as taken. If there's no tap, it reminds again, and if the dose still isn't confirmed, it's marked as missed. It double-checks. Not sure which bottle is which? Show the bottle to the camera. WeCare reads the label and tells you whether it's due now, scheduled for later, or already taken today, catching the most common mistakes: the wrong pill and a double dose. If the medication isn't on the senior's schedule at all, or the label can't be read clearly, WeCare doesn't guess. It says "I'm not sure about that one" so the senior knows not to take it until they check with their caregiver. It keeps the family in the loop. Every reminder, confirmation, missed dose, and scan is logged to the cloud. The WeCare caregiver app lets family members set up medications and schedules and see what was taken, what's coming up, and what was missed.

sections.heading: How we built it together!
sections.text: Hardware: a Raspberry Pi runs the device software in Python. A capacitive touch sensor on the Pi's GPIO pins handles confirmation. WeCare's voice is generated with ElevenLabs for a warm, natural-sounding voice that's easy for seniors to understand, and it plays through a JBL Bluetooth speaker. A scheduler (APScheduler) loads the senior's medications and fires reminders, repeats them, and marks doses as missed. We designed and 3D-printed a cute low-poly puppy sitting on a table that houses the electronics. AI bottle scanning: a Logitech USB webcam captures the bottle with OpenCV, and Google Gemini's vision model reads the label and matches it against the senior's medication list, returning structured results with a confidence level. Safety rules make sure WeCare never calls a medication "safe," only whether it matches the caregiver's schedule. Automatic retries and a fallback model keep it working when the AI service is busy. Caregiver app: designed in Figma and built with Expo (React Native) for a mobile-first caregiver experience.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Designing hardware around real parts. Fitting a Raspberry Pi, webcam, and wiring into something friendly-looking took several redesigns while working around the time our one 3D printer had.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We're proud of the full device loop working end to end: a spoken reminder, a tap to confirm, and the dose updating live in the cloud. Our AI bottle scan reads real labels and catches "wrong time" and "already taken" mistakes, and it says "I'm not sure" rather than guessing. We're also proud of how we came together as a team: merging hardware, AI, and app work built in parallel onto one shared design under real time pressure, and turning it into something that feels friendly enough to sit in someone's home.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned that designing for seniors means keeping things simple. Every feature had to work with a voice and a single tap, with no screens, menus, or passwords to remember. We also learned how much real-world details matter: a medication mistake isn't just forgetting; it's taking a pill twice, at the wrong time, or grabbing the wrong bottle, so WeCare had to handle all of those, not just send reminders. As a team, we learned the importance of agreeing on a shared plan early. We built the hardware, AI, and app in parallel, and bringing them together taught us to communicate constantly and settle on one design before building too far. We also learned that AI is powerful but needs guardrails: WeCare should never guess when someone's health is involved, so knowing when to say "I'm not sure" was just as important as getting the answer right. Finally, we learned that hardware makes ideas feel real. Hearing a friendly reminder and confirming it with a tap felt completely different from clicking through an app, and it showed us how technology can feel caring instead of complicated.

sections.text: Next, we want to fully connect the caregiver app to live data from the device so families see every dose update in real time and add phone alerts when a dose is missed. We'd love to add refill reminders and weekly summaries for caregivers and pharmacists. We also want to make WeCare work for more people by supporting multiple languages, improving recognition of real pharmacy labels, and expanding beyond seniors to anyone who has trouble keeping track of medications, such as people with memory, attention, or vision challenges. sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Hybrid and work-from-home environments have reshaped how UX teams collaborate, but they’ve also introduced new challenges: fragmented workflows, endless context-switching, digital fatigue, and a lack of cohesion across tools. Burnout isn’t caused by doing too much work, it’s caused by doing disorganized work without clarity or support. We wanted to rethink the workday not by adding another app, but by connecting the tools UX teams already rely on. Our goal was to create a system that reduces cognitive load and builds truly intelligent and connected workstreams.

sections.heading: Identifying the Challenge
sections.text: Through secondary research, Reddit discussions, surveys, interviews with employees, and insights shared during the Design-a-thon workshops, we uncovered a clear pain point: Employees are overwhelmed by scattered tool ecosystems and lose hours every week piecing their workflow together." Key root causes we identified: Excessive context-switching across platforms Important information buried in threads or outdated files Burnout linked to inefficient, fragmented workflows Lack of visibility between individual tasks and team-level goals Cognitive overload from juggling resources instead of ideating We realized the problem wasn’t motivation or discipline, it was a disjointed information environment.

sections.heading: Our Solution - What it does
sections.text: Aero is an AI assistant that transforms scattered workflows from a multitude of applications into one seamless flow, allowing UX professionals to spend less time searching for the necessary resources, and more time ideating/creating. Here is what it does: 1. Search & Surface Anything Instantly: Aero pulls relevant files, messages, comments, tasks, and references from across your ecosystem, all in one place. 2. Streamline Workflow With AI Summaries: Whether it’s a Slack thread, a Figma comment chain, or meeting notes, Aero condenses noise into clear next steps. 3. Automate Routine Admin Tasks: Organize your sprint priorities; Highlight blockers; Suggest relevant design resources; Collect related documents automatically. 4. Reduce Burnout Through Smart, Connected Work: By minimizing context-switching and cognitive load, Aero gives designers more time to ideate, explore, and create. 5. Maintain Trust With Privacy & Accessibility: User-controlled data permissions; Clear transparency about what Aero accesses; Inclusive design for all hybrid workers

devpost_page.title: Document Analysis Toolset
devpost_page.tagline: The Document Analysis Toolset uses custom trained vision models to analyze PDF files and extract signatures, detect forgery, show detailed version history, and identify manipulated areas of documents.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Document fraud costs organizations billions annually, with forged signatures and manipulated PDFs becoming increasingly sophisticated. Traditional manual verification methods are time-consuming, subjective, and often miss subtle digital alterations. I was inspired by real-world cases where: - Legal contracts were invalidated due to undetected signature forgeries - Financial institutions lost money to document manipulation - Court cases hinged on proving document authenticity My goal: democratize advanced document forensics using AI.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: The Document Analysis Toolset is a comprehensive AI-powered platform that provides three core forensic capabilities with models trained using HP AI Studio on NVIDIA GPUs. The system automatically detects and extracts signatures from PDF documents using YOLO-based object detection, processes multi-page documents in seconds, and allows users to download individual signature crops for further analysis. For signature verification, the deep learning classifier compares two signature images to determine authenticity with confidence scoring, providing side-by-side visual comparisons and expert-level accuracy in distinguishing genuine signatures from forgeries. The manipulation detection module utilizes Error Level Analysis (ELA) to identify digitally altered areas in PDF documents, highlighting suspicious regions and tracking version changes to reveal tampering attempts that would be invisible to the naked eye. The platform processes documents in real-time, supports multiple file formats, and presents results through clean, professional visualizations that make complex forensic analysis accessible to non-technical users.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: I built the system using a modern AI-first architecture. For the hosted web interface, I chose Streamlit for its rapid prototyping capabilities and clean presentation of complex data visualizations. The signature detection pipeline leverages a custom-trained YOLO model exported to ONNX format for optimized inference, while the forgery classification uses a fine-tuned Vision Transformer (ViT) model hosted on Hugging Face for the web versions, but both are also deployable for inference through HP AI Studio. My development workflow utilized HP AI Studio for model experimentation and training, with an NVIDIA GPU (RTX 4070 Ti Super) providing the computational power needed for deep learning model development. I implemented MLFlow for experiment tracking and model versioning, ensuring reproducible results and systematic performance improvements. The manipulation detection module integrates PDF2Image for document conversion and PIL for advanced image processing operations. Key technical decisions included using PyTorch with ONNX export for production deployment, implementing caching decorators for model loading optimization, and designing modular components that could be easily extended. I structured the codebase with separate pages for each analysis type, shared utility functions for common operations, and custom CSS styling for a professional user experience.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: One of the biggest challenges was optimizing model inference speed while maintaining accuracy. Initial implementations were too slow for real-time use, leading me to experiment with model quantization, ONNX optimization, and strategic caching. I also struggled with memory management when processing large PDF documents, ultimately implementing streaming approaches and efficient image handling. The signature detection model required extensive data preprocessing and augmentation to handle the wide variety of signature styles, document qualities, and scanning artifacts found in real-world documents.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: I successfully created a production-ready document forensics platform that rivals expensive specialized software, making advanced AI accessible through a simple web interface. The signature detection achieves over 95% precision across diverse document types, while the forgery classification model demonstrates over 90% accuracy in distinguishing authentic from forged signatures. The technical architecture is both scalable and maintainable, with clean separation of concerns and modular components that facilitate future development. The Error Level Analysis implementation successfully identifies subtle digital manipulations that would be missed by manual inspection, providing forensic investigators with a powerful new tool for document authentication. The entire system processes documents in real-time, making it practical for high-volume use cases in professional environments. Perhaps most importantly, this demonstrates that advanced AI capabilities can be democratized - bringing laboratory-grade document forensics to any professional who needs it, regardless of technical background or budget constraints.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: This project taught me valuable lessons about productionizing machine learning models and the importance of user-centered design in AI applications. I learned that model accuracy is only one piece of the puzzle - inference speed, memory efficiency, and result interpretability are equally crucial for real-world deployment.

sections.heading: What's next for Document Analysis Toolset
sections.text: My immediate roadmap includes expanding the signature verification model to handle a broader range of signature styles and document types, implementing ensemble methods to combine multiple detection approaches for higher accuracy, and adding support for additional document formats beyond PDF.
